prompt: Could you write a captivating short story beginning with the sentence: The old abandoned house at the end of the street held a secret that no one had ever discovered.
answer:
The old abandoned house at the end of the street held a secret that no one had ever discovered.

It was not the body beneath the kitchen floor. The police had found that in 1973.

Nor was it the money sewn into the nursery curtains. Burglars had discovered that one wet November and retired to Spain.

The secret was smaller than either of those things, and much harder to keep.

Every Thursday, at seventeen minutes past four, someone inside the house laughed.

Ada heard it on her way home from burying her husband.

It was his laugh.

She stopped beside the rusted gate, still holding the little paper bag of sandwiches the funeral director had insisted she take. For forty-two years, that laugh had embarrassed her in cinemas and startled birds from hedges.

She knew it as she knew her own name.

“Thomas?”

The house stood silent.

Ada returned the following Thursday.

At four sixteen, she felt foolish. At four seventeen, she heard him laughing so hard he could scarcely breathe.

Then her own voice, younger:

“You’ve put salt in it, you idiot.”

Their first flat. His disastrous birthday cake.

Ada gripped the gate until the laughter ended.

The next week, she brought a crowbar.

Inside, the house smelled of dust and apples. Wallpaper hung in long strips. On a table in the entrance hall stood a brass bell and a card.

*One room. One hour. Bring something you cannot replace.*

Beyond the table were three doors.

Ada had brought Thomas’s watch, which still lost six minutes every day. She laid it beside the bell and rang once.

The middle door opened.

Their kitchen waited on the other side.

Not the kitchen as it had been at the end, crowded with pill bottles and hospital leaflets. This was the yellow kitchen, before they painted it blue.

Thomas stood at the stove in his ridiculous apron.

“You’re late,” he said.

Ada made a sound she would never have permitted herself in public.

He turned. His smile faded.

“Oh, love.”

She crossed the room and held him.

He smelled of soap and onions. There was a small burn on his wrist. His heart beat against her cheek.

They sat at the table. Ada asked where he had been.

“Here,” he said. “It’s Thursday.”

She tried to explain the funeral, but he kept glancing toward the oven. At last she stopped. He served the casserole she had forgotten he used to make, and she ate a second helping while he watched, pleased.

When the kitchen clock struck five seventeen, she was standing in the dusty hall.

The watch was gone.

The following Thursday, she brought her wedding ring.

After that, the letters he had written from a job in Aberdeen. Then the chipped blue mug he would never let her throw away.

Each time, a door opened.

Once they were thirty, once fifty-six. Once she found him sitting on the bathroom floor with their newborn daughter asleep against his chest.

Ada knelt beside them.

“She’s so little,” she whispered.

Thomas looked exhausted and delighted.

“Apparently they get bigger.”

Ada laughed, then covered her mouth.

By winter, she had learned to save her questions for the last few minutes. Where did he go when she left? Did he know what happened to him? Could he come into the hall?

He never understood what she was asking.

Meanwhile, her daughter left increasingly worried messages.

*Mum, you missed Sunday lunch.*

*Mum, why is Dad’s desk gone?*

*Mum, please call me.*

Ada had begun taking things she could barely remember choosing: a seaside photograph, the wooden bird Thomas had carved, the recipe book full of his notes.

One Thursday, she arrived with the little red shoes their daughter had worn on her first birthday.

She placed them beside the bell.

Then she stood very still.

She remembered Thomas kneeling to buckle those shoes, his large fingers struggling with the tiny straps. But there was another memory: their daughter, grown now, kneeling in front of Ada before the funeral, fastening a buckle Ada couldn’t manage.

Ada picked up the shoes.

For the first time, the bell rang by itself.

All three doors opened.

Behind one, Thomas waited at twenty-three. Behind another, he was forty, holding two glasses of wine. Behind the third, he stood in the yellow kitchen.

“Coming?” he asked.

Ada took a step toward him.

“Can you come here instead?”

He smiled and held out his hand.

She looked down at the shoes.

“No,” she said.

The doors slammed so hard that plaster fell from the ceiling.

Outside, she sat on the front step and called her daughter. When the call connected, Ada had to wait a moment before she could speak.

“Have you eaten?” she asked.

That spring, the council demolished the house.

Ada watched from across the street. As the excavator broke through the entrance hall, she saw, briefly, a brass bell on a little table.

Beside it lay a watch, a ring, a blue mug.

She almost called out.

Then her granddaughter tugged her sleeve.

“Gran, look. A ladybird.”

Ada crouched beside her.

It was the smallest thing: six black spots on a bright red shell, crawling slowly across the child’s thumb.

Behind them, the house came down.

Ada stayed where she was until the ladybird flew.
